title: AI and your data
blurb: What happens to what you type, and what to keep out of AI tools.

slides.title: What you type goes somewhere
body: With most AI tools, your messages and any files you add are sent to the provider’s servers, where the model runs.
What happens next depends on the tool and its settings. Your data might be stored, reviewed, or used to train future models.

visual.caption: A general picture — every tool’s terms are different.

items.label: On your device
items.text: You type a message or paste in a document.

items.label: Provider’s servers
items.text: The model processes it and writes a reply.

items.label: Depending on the tool
items.text: It may be stored, logged, reviewed or used for future training.

slides.title: Think before you paste
body: Once something has been sent, you can’t take it back. Some kinds of information shouldn’t go into an AI tool unless it’s been approved for that use.
If you’re not sure, assume it doesn’t belong there.

visual.caption: Your organisation’s AI policy is the final word on what’s allowed.

items.heading: Personal information
items.text: Names, contact details and health information about real people.

items.heading: Secrets
items.text: Passwords, API keys and access tokens.

items.heading: Confidential material
items.text: Client or business information you’re not allowed to share.

slides.title: Not all AI tools are the same
body: The same model can come with very different terms. Personal or free accounts may handle data differently from tools your organisation has approved.
Approved tools have usually been checked for how data is stored, who can see it and whether it’s used for training.

visual.caption: Always check the specific tool’s terms and your organisation’s policy.
visual.question: Where should work information go?

cards.label: Personal or free account
cards.text: The terms may allow your chats to be stored or used to train future models.

cards.label: Approved work tool
cards.text: Your organisation has checked how data is handled, stored and protected.

slides.title: Habits that keep data safe
body: Most of the benefit of AI doesn’t need sensitive data at all. A little care keeps it that way.

visual.caption: Good habits for any AI tool.

items.heading: Use approved tools for work
items.text: Even if a personal tool is quicker to open.

items.heading: Remove identifying details
items.text: Swap real names and details for placeholders like “Person A”.

items.heading: Ask before you paste
items.text: If you’re unsure whether something is allowed, check first.

quiz.question: When you send a message to an online AI chatbot, where does it usually go?
options: To the provider’s servers, where the model runs
Nowhere — it’s deleted as soon as you send it
Only to your organisation’s IT team
quiz.explanation: Most AI tools send your input to the provider’s servers. What happens after that depends on the tool’s terms and settings.

quiz.question: Which of these is safest to paste into an AI tool that hasn’t been approved for work?
quiz.explanation: Public information carries little risk. Personal data, secrets and confidential documents should only go into tools approved for them.

quiz.question: You need AI help with a document that contains personal details. What’s a good approach?
options: Paste it into whichever tool is quickest
Use an approved tool, and remove or replace identifying details where you can
Split it across several chats so no single chat has everything
quiz.explanation: Approved tools and removing identifying details both reduce the risk. When in doubt, check your organisation’s policy.
